新宮市 Shingū

A city made by flows

Shingū at a glance

Shingū is a small city carrying a large region. The 2025 census counted 24,331 residents, 10% fewer than in 2020 and barely half the 1960 peak of 45,666; 40.3% are 65 or older, and in fiscal 2025 the city registered 109 births against 486 deaths. Since the 2005 merger with Kumanogawa the municipality covers 255 km², yet 96% of its people live in the former city on 31% of the land. The Kumanogawa valleys, the other 69%, hold 906.

The economy that built the town has changed form. Kumano timber was rafted down to Shingū until the mid-1960s, and the pulp and paper mill closed in 1995; health and welfare now employ one worker in five, trade another fifth, and farming, forestry and fishing 2.2%. The daytime population is 109% of the resident one because the region comes in to work, shop and be treated: the municipal medical centre (285 beds) serves about 100,000 people in three prefectures. Timber still dominates the port, as wood chips: 81% of its 1.19 million tonnes in 2024.

The name, “new shrine”, belongs to Kumano Hayatama Taisha, one of the three Kumano shrines. With Kamikura Shrine, the islet of Mifune-jima and the river itself it has been part of a World Heritage property since 2004. The Mizuno family governed the castle town for the Kishū Tokugawa from 1619 until the end of the Edo period. Shingū produced the poet Satō Haruo, the novelist Nakagami Kenji and the educator Nishimura Isaku. Its doctor Ōishi Seinosuke, executed in the High Treason case of 1911, was declared wrongly convicted by the city council in 2001 and made an honorary citizen in 2018.

It is also a hinge between regions: the junction where JR Central’s line from Nagoya (about 3 h 20 min) meets JR West’s from Shin-Ōsaka (about 4 h); a river-border town facing Kihō in Mie; and, by that village’s own account, the reason Kitayama, Japan’s only exclave village, chose Wakayama in 1871: its raftsmen lived off the Shingū timber trade.

Sources: census 2020/2025 (Statistics Bureau, e-Stat); Wakayama Prefecture; Shingū City profile; Shingū Municipal Medical Center; MLIT port statistics 2024; Agency for Cultural Affairs; honorary citizens; Wakayama on the High Treason case; Kitayama village.

The Kumano as one system

Shingū sits where one river system meets the sea. The flat map and the long profile show the same places: pick one in either and it lights up in both. The profile runs along the real bed of the Totsukawa–Kumano, from the Ōmine headwaters to the mouth, then on down the coast.

CONSTRAINT

Shingū occupies the narrow meeting ground of the Kii Mountains, Kumano River and Pacific Ocean while carrying the functions of a regional centre for southern Kumano. The same convergence that generated its prosperity also concentrates its exposure: major-river flooding, urban drainage failure, landslides, transport isolation, earthquake and Nankai Trough tsunami all intersect within a relatively small inhabited landscape.

STRATEGY

Concentrate + connect + accommodate + evacuate + coordinate

Urban functions are gathered into a compact hierarchy of centres; mountain communities remain connected through transport and local service nodes; development is progressively steered away from severe hazard; buildings and infrastructure accommodate recurring inundation; evacuation converts nearby elevation into life-safety infrastructure; river governance expands to the scale of the entire Kumano watershed.

LESSON

Resilience in Shingū is fundamentally spatial: each risk is addressed at the geographical scale that produces it, while those scales are coordinated into a single regional system.

1

Convergence created the city

concentrate

Shingū’s regional centrality is a direct expression of physical geography. The lower Kumano forms the outlet of a vast mountainous hinterland, while the Pacific opens the city toward maritime Japan. Goods, people, religious authority and political power accumulated precisely where these networks converged.

The medieval Shimohonmachi port settlement, located on a natural levee roughly two kilometres above the river mouth, already occupied this strategic interface. Archaeology has revealed underground warehouses, smithing activity, boat nails, river-access stairs and ceramics arriving from distant parts of Japan, evidence of a port integrated into long-distance maritime exchange and the economic sphere of the Kumano religious institutions.

Click the pulsing point on the map: the hall that stands on the site today, and a drawing of what was found.

The early city consequently emerged through several overlapping functions:

Each period reorganized movement while preserving Shingū’s basic role as an intermediary between interior and coast.

The castle itself embodied this relationship. Shingū Castle occupied Tankaku-yama (丹鶴山) above the river, while its Mizunote precinct descended toward a landing place and a row of charcoal warehouses. Mountain resources entered the city by river and continued toward coastal markets. The riverside economy extended into Kawaramachi, where merchants, inns, blacksmiths, restaurants, fishmongers, bathhouses and other businesses formed an intensely active commercial landscape. Historical documentation records almost 300 Kawaraya structures at its peak around the late Meiji and early Taishō periods.

Rail subsequently redirected urban movement. The Shingū Railway opened in 1913, a broad station approach reoriented the centre, and parts of the former castle moat were incorporated into the expanding twentieth-century city. The river-centred commercial morphology acquired a railway-centred layer; later road, medical and port development added further nodes. Shingū Port today remains Kinan’s only foreign-trade port, serving hinterlands extending into Mie and Nara while functioning simultaneously as a maritime gateway for Kumano tourism and cruise traffic.

The resulting city is best read as an urban palimpsest:

This historical layering matters for resilience because contemporary risk management operates within a landscape already structured by centuries of accumulated infrastructure, attachment and regional function.

2

Morphology, sacred landscape and adaptation

accommodate

Shingū’s physical form also reveals a distinctive relationship with environmental instability.

Kumano Hayatama Taisha, Kamikura Shrine, the river and the surrounding mountains belong to a sacred geography in which rock, water, forest and movement carry religious meaning. Pilgrimage connected these elements across the wider Kumano landscape; the river itself functioned historically as part of the approach toward Hayatama and today survives as a rare river pilgrimage route within the World Heritage landscape. Shingū’s tourism strategy (新宮市観光振興計画) continues to treat the Kumano River descent as a major cultural asset.

Physical geography therefore performs several functions at once:

That multiplicity gives Shingū’s vernacular flood architecture particular significance.

Kawaraya 川原家 — mobility

The Kawaraya of Kawaramachi were assembled from interlocking members without nails. During frequent floods, residents could dismantle them, move the components onto safer ground and rebuild once water levels receded. The city’s history of Kawaramachi speaks of sudden floods said to come five or six times a year and presents this highly reversible building form as a distinctive local response.

Its spatial principle is remarkably sophisticated:

retain economic access to the river by making architecture mobile.

The floodplain remained productive because permanence was transferred from the individual structure to the continuity of activity.

Agariya 上がり家 — redundancy

Elsewhere along the Kumano system, Agariya created a complementary form of resilience: secondary spaces on higher ground for storage, refuge and temporary occupation. Documented examples within present-day Shingū municipality include settlements such as Shingū, Hitari, Kujū and Shitaki.

Together, the two forms encode different strategies:

Both arose from an intimate reading of recurrent flood behaviour. Architecture absorbed hydrological variability directly into settlement practice.

Modern interventions reproduce the same logic at larger scales. Ring levees concentrate protection around selected settlements; building controls regulate residual exposure beyond them; urban pumps relocate water mechanically; tsunami planning organizes rapid movement toward elevation. The technologies have changed dramatically, yet the recurring spatial principles remain legible:

3

Four hazard pathways converge

evacuate · accommodate

Shingū’s risk geography becomes clearest when read directionally.

These pathways intersect during major events.

Kumano River: risk generated at regional scale

Shingū lies at the downstream end of a river system extending through Nara, Mie and Wakayama. Rainfall and slope processes occurring far beyond the municipality therefore materialize locally as river discharge, sediment and infrastructure pressure.

The 2011 Kii Peninsula disaster demonstrated this cascading geography with exceptional clarity. In Shingū, Typhoon Talas caused 13 deaths, one missing person and damage to 2,968 homes, including 81 destroyed or washed away. Municipal records also document widespread failures of electricity, communications, water, roads and river infrastructure.

The disaster unfolded as a chain:

Its geography exceeded every individual administrative sector.

Ichida-gawa: risk generated inside the city

The much smaller Ichida-gawa exposes a different hydraulic vulnerability. Rain falling over urban Shingū drains toward the Ichida and then the Kumano. During a major Kumano flood, high main-river levels impede this drainage and create the possibility of backflow. The sluice gate closes; urban water must then be pumped mechanically into the swollen river.

The central question becomes almost diagrammatic:

Where does the city’s rain go when the regional river is already full?

Following severe internal flooding during Typhoon 21 in 2017, national, prefectural and municipal authorities expanded the Ichida system. The reinforced national pumping station, in full operation from 2024, raised national pumping capacity from 17.1 to 28.0 m³/s, alongside additional prefectural and municipal drainage measures.

Ichida therefore turns a small urban tributary into an unusually clear illustration of hydraulic interdependence: local drainage performance depends on the state of a much larger river system.

Nankai Trough: elevation becomes infrastructure

The Pacific introduces another temporal regime entirely. Wakayama’s 2026 maximum-class scenario (地震動予測及び津波浸水想定（令和8年公表）) gives Shingū a reference maximum tsunami height of 13 m and approximately five minutes until a 1 m tsunami height at the modelled reference point.

Five minutes transforms topography into immediate life-safety infrastructure.

The hills embedded within Shingū’s urban fabric consequently possess overlapping functions: sacred prominence, urban landmark, landscape identity and potential refuge. Tsunami resilience depends as much upon route legibility, mobility and local knowledge as upon absolute elevation.

From the slopes: the hinterland cuts itself off

The fourth pathway runs down the valley walls. Shingū City contains 549 designated sediment-disaster warning zones, 495 of them special warning zones: 353 for steep-slope collapse, 189 for debris flow and 7 for landslides. They crowd the narrow valleys, where roads, river and houses share the same strip of flat ground.

In 2011 slopes failed across the three prefectures, releasing about 100 million m³ of sediment, the largest volume since the Second World War. Upstream the failures dammed rivers; in Shingū they cut roads. Route 168 and municipal roads broke at many points, isolating the whole of Takata, Ōga and Minami-Hizue and all of Kumanogawa-chō; supplies went in mainly by helicopter. The road to Takata reopened on 7 September, Route 168 between Miyai and Hongū on 11 September, and the last stretch from Miyai to the city on 14 October.

The pattern is old. In 1889, 1,080 slopes collapsed in the upper basin and 37 dammed lakes formed; at the mouth, the whole of Shingū town went under muddy floodwater.

Beyond the four pathways

The record adds slower pressures that the directional reading misses:

  • Heat. Shingū’s weather station set its record of 39.6 °C on 8 July 2024. Days of 35 °C or more averaged 2.4 a year in the 1990s and 11.3 a year in 2020–2025, with 23 in 2024 alone.
  • Rain intensity. The station’s records are 132.5 mm in one hour (4 September 2011) and 532.0 mm in one day (22 October 2017): the two floods this page keeps returning to.
  • Shaking and fire. J-SHIS gives a 75% chance of intensity 6-lower or stronger within 30 years at the city centre, and Wakayama expects 6-upper in both of its Nankai scenarios. After the 1946 Nankai earthquake, fire burned a third of the town.
  • Sediment and coast. Dams and breakwaters hold back sand the Kumano once delivered: Mie reports the Shichiri-mihama shoreline up to 80 m behind its 1947 line at Ida. Since 2011 the river also stays turbid for long periods after floods.
  • Drought and wildfire. No water restriction on the Kumano or on Shingū’s supply was found in the record, and no published wildfire statistics for the area.
Sources: JMA, Shingū station records and annual tables; J-SHIS (Y2024, average case); Wakayama, March 2026; Wakayama Prefecture on 1946; Mie Prefecture to MLIT; J-Power to MLIT, 2022.

4

Resilience through selective concentration

concentrate · connect

Demographic contraction adds another layer to the hazard problem. Shingū’s regional services must remain viable for an increasingly dispersed and ageing population, including mountain communities where transport corridors themselves are vulnerable to rainfall and slope failure.

The city’s 立地適正化計画, Location Optimization Plan, responds through a polycentric hierarchy:

  • Midorigaoka–Jōnan 緑丘・城南
    the principal urban centre, intended to retain complex higher-order functions for Shingū and the wider Kumano region;
  • Kōyō 光洋
    a regional node incorporating major medical and service functions;
  • Kumano-gawa 熊野川町 and Takata 高田
    living hubs whose role centres on everyday accessibility and the continuity of smaller mountain communities.

The planning logic combines concentration with connection. Higher-order services gain sufficient density to remain viable, while transport links maintain access from peripheral settlements. This becomes especially consequential in mountainous areas, where a single landslide can transform road accessibility into medical, social and logistical isolation.

Hazard exposure increasingly informs the geography of future development as well. Residential-inducement areas are adjusted as new landslide red zones are designated, gradually shifting where housing, services and investment receive planning priority.

The process works through temporal steering:

This allows demographic policy and hazard policy to operate through the same spatial framework.

The 2025 津波防災地域づくり推進計画, Tsunami Disaster-Resilient Community Development Promotion Plan strengthens that integration by building tsunami measures on the city’s comprehensive plan (総合計画), resilience plan (国土強靭化地域計画) and disaster plan (地域防災計画), and explicitly aligning them with the Urban Master Plan (都市計画マスタープラン) and Location Optimization Plan (立地適正化計画).

The implication is profound: tsunami adaptation enters ordinary urban planning, influencing the long-term configuration of the city alongside housing, transport and services.

5

Resilience extends beyond the resident population

evacuate · connect

Shingū’s regional role also produces a mobile population of pilgrims, visitors and cruise passengers whose relationship to the landscape differs sharply from that of residents.

Kumano tourism is inseparable from the same river, mountains and sacred topography that structure hazard. The city’s tourism strategy (新宮市観光振興計画) treats the World Heritage river pilgrimage, Kumano Kodō, urban heritage and mountain landscapes as interconnected resources; Shingū Port extends that network outward as a cruise and maritime gateway.

This creates a distinctive resilience requirement: people with limited local spatial knowledge must be able to understand risk quickly.

A resident may recognize the nearest high ground, remember previous inundation or understand which road disappears during heavy rain. A newly arrived pilgrim operates from a different knowledge base. Hazard communication therefore becomes part of destination management.

Shingū’s web hazard map integrates flood depth, tsunami inundation, landslide zones, shelters and evacuation timing and is available in Japanese, English, Chinese, Korean and Tagalog.

Tourism and disaster preparedness consequently meet through spatial legibility: the landscape must remain culturally rich while also becoming intelligible under emergency conditions.

The same principle applies to heritage itself. Shingū’s cultural assets carry the memory of earlier relationships with river and terrain. Kawaramachi records accommodation to flood; the medieval port records the economic geography of the river; the sacred sites preserve a cosmology rooted in mountains, rocks and water. Contemporary resilience therefore concerns the continuity of meaning and practice alongside physical safety.

Five places show the principle at work:

  • Mifune Matsuri 御船祭 (16 October): the deity’s boat is escorted up the Kumano to the islet of Mifune-jima, and nine small boats race around it. The rite needs a navigable river; the festival is a way of keeping the river part of the town’s life.
  • Oto Matsuri 御燈祭 (6 February): torch-bearers run down the 538 stone steps of Kamikura Shrine, whose object of worship is the rock Gotobiki-iwa. With the Hayatama festival it has been a national Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property since 2016.
  • Shimohonmachi under Tankaku Hall: the medieval port was found in 2015 because a cultural hall was planned there. The hall moved onto the already-disturbed part of the plot, storage pits were kept in place beneath it, and the grounds became a National Historic Site in 2022. The same building is a designated tsunami evacuation site: memory and refuge on one plot.
  • Mizunote 水ノ手: excavation below the castle found about 20 charcoal storehouses and a landing. The domain’s income was stacked on the riverbank.
  • Kawaramachi 川原町: the riverbed town was gone by 1950; a rebuilt Kawaraya alley beside Hayatama keeps its demountable form legible to visitors.

Hover a name to find it on the map; pulsing points open photographs.

6

The watershed defines the governance scale

coordinate

Shingū’s most consequential planning lesson emerges when administrative geography is compared with hazard geography.

The city governs only the downstream fragment of the system producing its largest floods. Hydrologically, the operative region is:

Flood governance therefore expands outward through 流域治水, basin-wide flood management. The contemporary framework combines national river authorities, prefectures, municipalities, dam operators, electricity companies, forest management, sabō, land-use policy and local preparedness. The 2022 river improvement plan (新宮川水系河川整備計画), building on the 2021 basin-wide flood-management project (新宮川水系流域治水プロジェクト), explicitly combines channel works with land-use regulation, adaptations in residential form and enhancement of basin storage functions.

Its interventions operate at different points in the same system:

This basin logic becomes particularly important under climate change.

In 2021, the Shingū and Gokase river systems became Japan’s first basic river-policy revisions (河川整備基本方針) explicitly incorporating projected climate-driven increases in rainfall together with the emerging basin-wide flood-management framework. MLIT described the change as a shift from planning based on historical rainfall toward planning that incorporates future climatic intensification.

Shingū therefore sits at the intersection of two major transitions:

The city’s resilience increasingly depends upon decisions made far upstream, decades ahead and across multiple institutions.

Synthesis · one city, several geographies

Shingū becomes most legible when its overlapping spatial systems are placed side by side. Each map below is drawn at its own scale — zoom any of them.

Each produces a different territorial logic. Resilience emerges from their coordination.

The historical continuity

  • Kawaraya moved architecture.
  • Agariya displaced critical household functions uphill.
  • Pumps move urban water.
  • Tsunami planning moves people toward elevation.
  • Location planning shifts future development.
  • Watershed governance shifts decision-making upstream.

Across radically different technologies and institutions, the same underlying intelligence recurs: preserve function by allowing spatial relationships to adjust to environmental change.

That is the distinctive resilience logic of Shingū.

A city whose prosperity, spirituality and danger arise from the same flows learns to endure by governing movement: of water, sediment, buildings, people, investment and authority, each at the scale where movement can actually be shaped.

In brief

Constraints

The city has to remain the functional centre of a much larger region while occupying one of that region’s most constrained and exposed pieces of land. Its planning problem is therefore fundamentally contradictory: concentrate people and services enough to sustain a shrinking regional population, maintain connections with remote mountain communities, and preserve Shingū’s role as the service centre of southern Kumano, while progressively reducing exposure to river flooding, internal flooding, landslides and a future Nankai Trough tsunami.

Strategy

Nested spatial system:

regional centre + compact urban hubs + connected peripheral settlements + gradual hazard-sensitive land-use steering + basin-scale flood management beyond municipal boundaries.

Lesson

Resilience depends on choosing the correct geographical scale for each problem and then connecting those scales together.

Regional Centre

Shingū’s regional centrality emerged directly from its geography.

At the mouth of the Kumano River, it became the natural transfer point between the mountainous interior and maritime Japan: timber, charcoal and other goods moved downstream from the Kii Mountains, then outward through Ikeda port at the river mouth toward Edo and other markets. This river–sea junction supported early urban concentration around Kumano Hayatama Taisha, later reinforced by Shingū’s role as a castle town and administrative centre, still called 熊野の都, the metropolis of Kumano, in the city’s Urban Planning Master Plan (都市計画マスタープラン).

Its position also links three overlapping hinterlands across Wakayama, Mie and Nara, whose river-basin communities long shared economic and social networks beyond prefectural boundaries. Modern infrastructure consolidated this role. The Shingū Railway opened in 1913, the station reorganized the urban core, and Shingū Port remains the Kinan region’s principal foreign-trade port.

The result is a strong historical path dependence in which transport, administration, commerce, health care and other higher-order services continue to concentrate in Shingū. The same river mouth, coastal lowland and mountain interface that generated this centrality now concentrate its exposure to flooding, tsunami, landslides and transport disruption, making regional centrality and disaster vulnerability products of the same geography.

Kamikura mountain foot · a micro-morphology

One small piece of ground holds every system in this essay at once. At the foot of Kamikura-yama the sacred mountain and its stone steps, the city’s drainage channel at the head of the Ichida-gawa system, a row of temples and houses, a school compound and the town grid touch within a few hundred metres. This last chapter reads that ground plot by plot, on GSI’s 1 m laser elevation model, layer by layer: the ground (下部構造), the lots (中部構造), the buildings and open spaces on them (上部構造) and what flows through (流れ).

Drawn by rules, not as a box. West: 25 m upslope of the break of slope, so the forest edge, the slope and the steep ground behind the plots are inside. East: the street that bounds the compound of 神倉小学校 (Kamikura Elementary School). North: the lane that closes the first full block above the school and the temple row. South: the street just south of the shrine entrance, so the entrance, the bridge and the foot of the steps are inside and the climb to Gotobiki-iwa is not.

下部構造 · micro-relief微地形

The mountain does not grade into the town; it stops: 40° above the foot, 1° below it. Across the 25 m strip inside the west edge the ground rises 22.6 m (median; at most 33.8 m), then the plain stays near 6.6 m. In the town the bare-earth model finds no step of 1 m or more outside the buildings and the channel; every such step lies on the mountain face above the foot.

中部構造 · plots町割・屋敷割

The Ministry of Justice parcel map here is a digitised cadastral drawing in arbitrary coordinates (任意座標系); fitted to GSI’s road edges, its road parcels sit a median 1.2 m from them. On the median its numbered parcels stop at the foot of the mountain; row by row the edge wanders (the middle half of the rows from 10 m upslope to 12 m out). Buildings are coloured by the alignment test below.

中部構造 · precincts境内

The sacred properties sit between the slope and the channel: the shrine’s lower precinct at the entrance (1,217 m² inside the line); north of it 妙心寺, one of the hongan temples that administered Kamikura-yama, thought to have led the Kumano bikuni, the nuns who raised funds for the Kumano shrines; and the Zen temple 宗応寺 further north. Across the channel, on the town side, lie the grounds of the 出雲大社新宮教会 (734 m²), a separate body.

上部構造 · everyday life生活

Houses on small plots fill the blocks between precincts, school and streets: 126 of the 127 footprints are mapped as ordinary buildings (普通建物); the one robust building (堅ろう) is the school’s.

上部構造 · public space現代公共空間

The school compound is the one large open ground: 1.20 ha inside the line, nearly a quarter of it, along the east bank of the channel. Its building is an emergency refuge for earthquake and tsunami (third floor, 14.3 m), its gym a core shelter. Across the channel two private projects turn old plots into public space: Youth Library えんがわ (2013), a library in an old house, and おいしいパーク (2020–2022), a vegetable field opened as a park and reading place for it.

流れ · water水系

神倉堀端都市下水路, the Kamikura Horibata Urban Drainage Channel: a municipal drainage channel in the upper Ichida-gawa system, crossing the area as an open, stone-faced channel cut up to 3.2 m below the plain. It comes in from the north on the town grid, cuts diagonally past the school and reaches the mountain only at the shrine entrance, where the stream from Kamikura-yama joins it after falling from 63.5 m to 4.7 m in 170 m. The headwater watercourse is also documented as Kamikura-gawa.

流れ · paths道

The streets keep to the town grid. The pedestrian routes do not: the 538 steps of the steep 男坂 (Otoko-zaka) and the gentler 女坂 (Onna-zaka) climb from the entrance, and the bridge over the channel is the threshold between town and mountain.

流れ · hazard災害

83.3% of the area lies in a sediment-disaster warning zone, 15.2% in a special one. Two hazards overlap: slope failure on the 千穂ヶ峰 and 神倉 slopes (35.1%) and debris flow from the gullies above the shrine entrance (神倉川右支渓, 59.3%), a zone that fans out east across the school ground. 84.7% is inside the maximum assumed river flood. The residential-inducement area of the Location Optimization Plan covers 32.9% and stops short of the slope.

流れ · sacred信仰

Gotobiki-iwa, where, by tradition, the Kumano gods first came down, lies outside the area, 330 m up the line. Inside it lies the threshold: the shrine’s lower precinct, the 下馬 stone, the 天磐盾 stele and the 猿田彦神社・神倉三宝荒神社 at the foot, and the last 20 m of the steps the torches run down every 6 February. Arrows at the edge point to 熊野速玉大社 (0.9 km), 阿須賀神社 (1.3 km) and the mouth of the Kumano (2.8 km).

下部構造 · groundWhere does Kamikura-yama stop?

The 1 m model holds here. Every cell of the study area comes from GSI’s 1 m laser model (DEM1A); in the whole 1.3 × 0.9 km frame only 535 cells fall back to the 5 m model. It agrees with the GSI survey marks within 800 m of the study area: two of three levelling benchmarks to within 0.01 m and 0.14 m (the third reads 0.79 m low), the two triangulation points to within 0.08 m and 0.51 m. On open, flat ground the 5 m model agrees with it (median difference 0.9 cm, spread 3.5 cm), but it reads the channel as 0.93 m deep where the 1 m model reads 2.68 m: at 5 m the ditch that organises the foot all but disappears. The caveat is the buildings: 28% of the study area lies under a GSI outline, where bare ground is interpolated.

Four ways to find the foot. On 310 cross-profiles, one every 2 m along 618 m of the front, the foot is located four ways: as the edge of the mountain mask (A), the first point 1 m above the profile’s own plain (B), the most concave point (C) and the knee of a two-segment line fitted to the profile (D). A and B both rest on a threshold 1 m above a plain, and they agree most closely (a median 1.5 m apart). Their median is the foot on the map; their spread is the band around it. The four agree within 5 m on 46.5% of the profiles; their median spread is 5.8 m, but on a tenth of the profiles it exceeds 31 m, and each lies a median 0.9–2.4 m from their common line. Where they agree, the answer is a line: above it the ground rises at a median 40°, below it at 1°. The face stays steep almost to the foot: on 46% of the profiles the steepest metre of the last six climbs at 45° or more (on 66% ten metres higher up), and then the ground flattens.

下部構造 · groundWhat follows the foot? Measured, not assumed

The foot runs N 1° E along the 618 m measured and N 7° E over the 0.9 km of the frame; the town grid runs N 5° E: at the scale of the town, foot, grid and compass coincide, so the grid’s orientation alone cannot say whether the mountain or the compass drew it. The test therefore uses the places where the foot bends. Wherever its local direction differs from the town grid by 10° or more, each piece of a feature (at most 10 m long) counts for whichever of the two it is closer to, parallel or square. Chance comes from sliding the foot’s directions along the foot by 50 m or more, so that its bends meet features they did not shape; shuffling single pieces instead would treat neighbouring pieces as independent and make chance too easy to beat. A run counts as significant only if the result also holds when the slide is at least 100 m. Every test is rerun with each of the four foot definitions and with a second registration of the parcel map: six runs, which check that a result does not hang on those choices (they are not independent samples).

Within 25 m, the channel and the lanes bend with the mountain. The channel’s centre line follows the foot’s bends in 6 of the 6 runs, the lanes in 4. Where the channel runs along the foot, around the shrine entrance and south of it (250 m, 94 m of them inside the study area), its east–west wiggles track the foot’s (correlation 0.82) at about half their amplitude. Other lines lean the same way without holding: the channel’s banks, the back boundaries of the plots (8 of the 9 lines that can be tested) and the buildings are significant in only 3 of the six runs. Frontages, temple, shrine and church grounds, the drawn waterway and the steep steps on the foot face show nothing (0 of 6). Beyond 25 m, nothing holds but two frontages in one place, 50–100 m out from the foot just north of the study area (5 of 6 runs); every other class reaches at most 2 of 6. The terrain draws the edge of the town and, within 25 m of it, the channel and the lanes; the grid draws the rest.

中部構造 · lotsThe parcel map on the ground

The Ministry of Justice map for 千穂 and 神倉 (登記所備付地図データ, sheet 「新宮・千穂一丁目・神倉一丁目他」) is a digitised cadastral drawing in arbitrary coordinates (任意座標系). Its roads (道) and waterways (水) are unnumbered strips of their own; every other parcel carries a lot number (地番), whoever owns it. The strips make it possible to place the drawing: the school parcel (715-3) matched to the school’s outline gives a first position; the road parcels fitted to GSI’s 1:2,500 road edges give the final one. To fit, the drawing has to be enlarged by 13–16% and turned 14° (31% more area than drawn); its road parcels then lie a median 1.2 m from the road edges (58% within 1.5 m). Records descended from the Meiji land-tax surveys, in which residents measured their own land and drew the village maps, are said to run short (縄伸び): in the cadastral surveys certified from FY1970 to FY2011, MLIT finds surveyed areas 26% larger than registered ones on average, roads and waterways excluded. That compares registers, not drawings, but it points the same way. Positions stay approximate; directions are what the test above uses.

Two results do not depend on those details. On the median, the numbered parcels end at the foot: their western edge lies a median 0.3 m from it (−1.7 m to +0.9 m across the six runs), though row by row it wanders, the middle half of the rows between 10 m upslope and 12 m out. And the map’s waterway parcels keep a course of their own, a median 35.5 m out from the foot (the middle half of the rows 21–46 m): numbered parcels fill the strip between the mountain and that line, a single parcel deep on half the rows. 宗応寺’s address point falls 4.0 m inside parcel 708-1, with the next numbered parcel 7.5 m away, so the test counts that parcel as temple property; 妙心寺’s lies inside the school parcel, 0.8 m from its edge, among small parcels, so its plot cannot be identified at this accuracy and is left out.

流れ · flowsOne flow, several names

The channel through the study area is 神倉堀端都市下水路, the Kamikura Horibata Urban Drainage Channel: a municipal drainage channel in the upper Ichida-gawa system. The headwater watercourse is also documented as Kamikura-gawa (神倉川). Shingū’s master plan lists it among the city’s urban drainage channels (都市下水路), apart from its entry for the river Ichida-gawa (河川). The names belong to different systems — hydrology, river administration, urban drainage — and overlap; none of them marks a legal point where one becomes the next.

  1. 千穂ヶ峰Chihogamine, the source
  2. 神倉川Kamikura-gawa: the headwater name in a 1997 prefectural assembly record, the city’s disaster plan (市田川神倉川右支渓) and MLIT’s purification transfer of 2000, which feeds it 0.3 m³/s of Kumano water
  3. 神倉堀端都市下水路Kamikura Horibata Urban Drainage Channel: municipal storm drainage; 59.7 ha catchment, 779 m planned, 450 m improved (2012)
  4. 市田川Ichida-gawa: a Class A river since 1970; MLIT describes it as rising on 千穂ヶ峰 and running 4.8 km to the Kumano (basin 5.36 km²)
  5. 熊野川the Kumano

Width. Municipal design width: 1.5–2.0 m (the plan’s 管径巾員). GIS-measured visible channel: about 3.5 m. GIS-measured wall-to-wall corridor: about 4–5 m. The municipal figure and the GIS measurements refer to different definitions of channel width; no engineering cross-section has yet been located.

  1. FY1959 Shingū starts building urban drainage channels for storm water.
  2. 1970–1975 The Ichida-gawa becomes a Class A river (1970); its lowest 2 km pass to direct national control (1972); the prefecture designates further land as river area along it and the Ukishima-gawa (1975, under River Act art. 6(1)(iii); the maps are not published online).
  3. FY1999 MLIT’s national sewerage project archive records landscape works on 神倉堀端都市下水路 completed in FY1999 (平成11), including 740 m² of stone facing, scenic safety railings and 124 m of planting, listed under two model programmes (水循環・再生下水道モデル事業 and 水環境保全共同事業).
  4. 2012 The master plan counts 450 of its 779 planned metres as improved.
  5. 2025–2026 The FY2025 budget carries ¥4.53 million for the channel’s repair (神倉堀端下水路改修事業); stone-facing repair in 千穂 (30 m² of wall facing, a landscaping licence required) is tendered in August and again in September 2025, the works due by February 2026.

The channel and the parcel map disagree. Where the map covers it (from 64 m north of the study area to 34 m before the channel leaves it), today’s channel takes three courses. In the north (135 m) it runs in the map’s strips of road and waterway (59–71%; none of it inside a numbered parcel). Then for 79 m it cuts diagonally through numbered parcels (90–95%), 65–70% of it more than 3 m inside them, beyond the registration’s error: half through the school’s parcel, up to 11–13 m from its edge, the rest through two others. In the south (about 100 m) it runs along the edge of the school parcel, at most 3–5 m inside it, and within 3 m of the map’s waterway for 40–65% of its length. The ranges are the two registrations. The drainage channel follows the grid, cuts through the parcels, then returns towards the drawn waterway along the foot.

流れ · flowsTransect: Gotobiki-iwa → the steps → the channel → houses → national road → city hall

One line runs through the area: from the summit shrine at Gotobiki-iwa (ground at 88.3 m on the 1 m model; the rock itself is about 11 m high) down the path and the 538 steps to the bridge at their foot (6.6 m), then due east across the town to the city hall (8.5 m), 1,132 m in all. The first 331 m are mountain. Outside the channels, the town part lies between 3.7 m and 8.6 m; it dips to 2.1 m in the Ukishima-gawa channel and rises again towards the city hall.

流れ · sacredWhere the landscape itself became sacred

Where the gods first came down. Kumano Hayatama Taisha places the first descent of the Kumano gods on Gotobiki-iwa, the boulder on Kamikura-yama (gotobiki is the local word for a toad). From there, in the shrine’s account, they moved to 石淵 across the river (now 貴祢谷) and, in the 58th year of Emperor Keikō, to the present site, which was therefore called 新宮, the “new shrine”, with Kamikura as its 元宮, the original seat. The city gives this origin of the name only as one that “is also said” (ともいわれています). The cliff under the rock is identified with the 天磐盾 that Jimmu climbs at 熊野神邑 in the Nihon Shoki; the shrine on it enshrines 高倉下命 and 天照大御神 and belongs to Hayatama as a subsidiary shrine (摂社).

Gongen-yama: gods in the form of Buddhas. Kamikura-yama is the southern peak of 権現山, a name the city glosses as “the mountain where Hayatama’s god appears provisionally” (権に現れる). In Hayatama’s words, the worship of the Kumano Gongen spread as that of “gods appearing provisionally in the form of Buddhas” (神が仮に仏の姿をかりて現れる), and by around the 10th century the Kumano gods were worshipped as the twelve Kumano Gongen (熊野十二社（所）大権現). UNESCO’s statement of the property’s value reads its sites, routes and forests as a cultural landscape of the fusion of Shinto, “rooted in the ancient tradition of nature worship”, and Buddhism, with Shugendō, “influenced by the former two faiths”, as a third element; the nomination lists Gotobiki-iwa first among the most typical natural objects where gods were held to descend. The rock carries the layers itself. Fragments of a late-Yayoi bronze bell found around it have been a prefectural property since 2012; repairs to the stone walls when the shrine was rebuilt in 1956 turned up about 300 Buddhist objects from three spots around the rock, late Heian to Muromachi: mirrors, sutra containers, a gilt-bronze Kannon, sutra stones written one character each. Since the Heian period, Shugendō practitioners training on the mountain had built sutra mounds around it.

The climb as a sequence of thresholds. From the town the way crosses the channel by the 下馬 stone (1672: a pillar telling riders to dismount here; a pilgrim from Ōshū gave it to mark his seven pilgrimages to the three Kumano shrines), passes the shrines and steles at the foot and climbs 538 stone steps, laid, by tradition, as Minamoto no Yoritomo’s gift in 1193 (鎌倉積み). On the 1 m model the mapped steps rise 71.2 m over 218.5 m on the map: 26.1° on average from the foot to 中ノ地蔵堂, 11.2° above it, 39.1° over the steepest 10 m, 44 m from the foot. Above them the path climbs about 11 m more over 110.6 m to the rock. A stone at the foot carries a poem by Fujiwara no Saneuji from the imperial anthology 続古今和歌集 (1265) that already speaks of the climb: 「三熊野の神倉山の石たゝみ のぼりはてゝも 猶祈るかな」, the stone way of Kamikura-yama climbed to its end, and still a prayer. Thresholds are where meaning is written down: of the 21 steles, boards and shrines that OpenStreetMap maps within 12 m of the line, 15 stand in its last 41 m.

6 February: the fire comes down. The Oto Matsuri is Kamikura’s annual festival; the city describes it as carrying “the tradition of the Kumano yamabushi since ancient times” and calls it a Shugendō fire festival. In the 2024 programme the priests and their attendants leave Hayatama at 17:50 and reach Kamikura at 18:20; the sacred fire is kindled at 19:10; at about 19:25 the great torch goes down to 中ノ地蔵堂 and back while the climbers (上り子) are shut inside the gate; at about 20:00 the gate opens and they run down the steps with the fire in their torches. Afterwards the priests go on to 阿須賀神社 (about 21:40) and back to Hayatama (about 22:10); the next afternoon mochi are thrown on the school ground. By day the climbers, in white with straw rope, visit Hayatama, 阿須賀神社, 妙心寺 and others. The city speaks of about 2,000; the organisers counted 1,580 in 2026; women do not climb. Hayatama gives the festival’s meaning as receiving the god’s fire into each torch at the old new year and bringing the god into each household, to light the household altar and the hearth. With the shrine’s own festival, 新宮の速玉祭, it has been an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property since March 2016.

Mountain, town, river, sea. Measured on one line, the order falls from mountain to river: the ground at the rock at 88 m, the bridge at the foot of the steps at 6.6 m, Hayatama on higher ground, about 12 m (on the 5 m model), the river, near sea level, 294 m beyond it, 3.0 km above its mouth. The gods’ path, in the shrine’s account, leaves the line: from the rock across the river to 石淵, then back to Hayatama’s riverside site. The water runs down it by another way: the stream from Kamikura-yama joins 神倉堀端都市下水路 at the shrine entrance, and 市田川 carries it east through the town into the Kumano’s estuary, 0.4 km from the mouth. The city reads Hayatama’s own god, 熊野速玉大神, as the force of water made divine (水の勢いを神格化したものと考えられています). The river is itself part of the inscribed pilgrimage route: pilgrims on the Nakahechi mostly came down from Hongū by boat to Hayatama, then went from 阿須賀神社 to 浜王子 and over 高野坂 to Nachi; the city lists the Kumano and 御船島, where Hayatama’s god goes upriver by boat every 16 October, as World Heritage under the Nakahechi.

Layers, not a single origin. In the Middle Ages the mountain was run by shrine monks (神倉聖) and four hongan temples (本願), the fund-raisers for its upkeep. One of them, 妙心寺, a nunnery at the foot, administered Kamikura-yama under the Shingū hongan; in 1531 its nun 妙順尼 was granted the hongan title after a restoration funded by collections in the provinces. A copy of the Nachi pilgrimage mandala, the kind the Kumano bikuni are said to have carried and explained, is known as 妙心寺旧本 (now kept at Hayatama). The decrees separating kami from Buddhas (1868) and abolishing Shugendō (1872) cut through this: the Kumano shrines became Shinto only, and the hongan temples nearly all closed; 妙心寺 survives beside the shrine office. Later layers were added at the foot: the 天磐盾 stele of 1990, for the 2,650th year of the imperial era; 猿田彦神社・神倉三宝荒神社, built in 1983 and rebuilt in 2024, shrines to Sarutahiko, who guided Ninigi’s descent and is a god of crossroads in the Nihon Shoki, and to Sanbō Kōjin, guardian of the Three Treasures, worshipped in Shugendō and kept in homes as the god of the hearth; until the Meiji period a Sarutahiko shrine, known as Tengu-sama, stood on the mountain. The donation that rebuilt them in 2024 also paid for renewing or repairing 満山社, 火神社 and 中ノ地蔵堂, for the 20th anniversary of the World Heritage listing.

A living landscape is a remade one. UNESCO’s statement records rites of Shinto, Buddhism and Shugendō “still underway even now”. Here they are also made and unmade. 神州院, a temple in the town, held an Ōmine fire rite with fire-walking at Kamikura on the day after the festival from the end of the Shōwa era; the 32nd, in 2019, was the last there. At Nachi, Seiganto-ji, whose head priest revived Kumano Shugendō in 1988, rebuilt in 2023, on a new site, the Gyōjadō (行者堂) of Kumano Shugendō demolished in the early Meiji years, about 150 years before, and closed it for three days of Shugendō practice (19–21 June 2026). Read along the climb, the sequence is spatial as well as temporal: the oldest finds came from around the rock; the 下馬 stone of 1672 and the stele of 1990 stand at the foot, where the town meets the mountain.

  • Method: the edges, the break of slope, the ground layers, the mountain foot, the registration of the parcel map, the alignment test and the transect are rebuilt by kansai/tools/kamikura/. The break of slope (the west edge’s rule, and definition A of the foot) is the edge of ground at least 1 m above the plain of the whole frame (6.05 m, the median of near-flat ground) and steeper than 12° (or 3 m above it), connected to the slopes above 40 m. A building’s direction is the long side of its smallest enclosing rectangle; lines are cut into pieces of at most 10 m, and a boundary shared by two parcels counts once. Chance comes from sliding the foot’s sequence of directions along the foot by every offset of at least 50 m and recomputing the share each time, so that neighbouring pieces, which are not independent, move together; a run counts only if the result also holds with a minimum offset of 100 m.

Method and known imperfections

  • Projection JGD2011 / Japan Plane Rectangular CS VI (EPSG:6674), computed exactly in the page; web tiles are reprojected corner by corner. Statistics use unsimplified polygons; the maps are simplified. Building counts test one point inside each footprint against the hazard areas as drawn.
  • Every approximation, correction and unverified statement is logged in kansai/CAVEATS.md; the build pipeline is in kansai/tools/.
